extracted.intended_audience: software engineering researchers and practitioners (developers, team leads, and tool builders) interested in empirical studies of code/peer review practices
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation and characterization of contemporary (lightweight, tool-supported) software peer review practices across industrial and open-source projects, including measurable parameters (interval, size, participants, effectiveness, knowledge sharing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review process (inspection vs RTC vs CTR vs tool-supported)
rubrics_metrics.description: What peer review process (e.g., Fagan inspection vs Commit-then-review) does the project use?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper enumerates three types: traditional software inspection (Fagan-style: planning, overview, preparation, inspection, reworking, follow-up), OSS email-based review (patch posted to mailing list; review-then-commit (RTC) common; some projects permit trusted commit-then-review (CTR)), and lightweight tool-supported review (e.g., Gerrit, CodeFlow, CodeCollaborator). Each has different traceability and workflow characteristics: Gerrit uses Verify/Approve/Submit stages; CodeFlow stores comments, sign-offs, and thread statuses; CodeCollaborator supports assignment, business rules (e.g., require 2 reviewers) and suggestions based on recent file editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review interval (time-to-complete)
rubrics_metrics.description: How long do reviews take (from submission to completion)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured using 'first response' and 'full interval' heuristics (for tool data, review considered complete at last activity). Contemporary projects show short intervals (median on order of hours to about a day). Examples: AMD median 17.5 hours; Microsoft Bing 14.7h, Office 18.9h, SQL 19.8h; Chrome 15.7h, Android 20.8h. Implication: reviews should be quick to be frequent and fit iterative development.

rubrics_metrics.name: First response time
rubrics_metrics.description: How long until the first reviewer activity / response occurs after submission?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-response is a distinct metric showing reviewer attentiveness; most reviews are picked up within a few hours, indicating reviewers regularly monitor review streams. Use as indicator of reviewer availability and responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review frequency (reviews per month)
rubrics_metrics.description: How often are reviews performed (e.g., reviews per month)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects differ by adoption stage and lifecycle: categorized trends include adoption (ramping up, e.g., Bing), cyclic (release-driven, e.g., Office, Android), and stable (consistent review volume, e.g., Chrome, SQL). Median reviews-per-month statistics and time-series trends indicate team-level adoption and cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifact/change size (lines and files changed)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the size of the artifact under review (e.g., lines changed, number of files)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller changes enable shorter review intervals. Paper reports medians: OSS projects (Apache, Linux) medians 11–32 lines; Lucent inspections median 263 lines; Android and AMD median 44 lines; Chrome median 78 lines (includes median 5 files). Distribution is left-skewed for many projects (majority small changes) with long tails for larger changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reviewers (invited and participating)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many reviewers are involved in a review (invited vs actually participating)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as invited reviewers and number of participants (excluding author). The median number of participants is typically two. Authors often invite 3–4 reviewers and the actual active participants commonly settle at about 2. Teams may then invite additional reviewers during a round if complexity or risk requires more eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection technique (self-selection vs assignment; tool suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: How are reviewers chosen (developers self-select, assignment, invitations, tool-suggested based on file history)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSS often relies on self-selection (broadcasting a change to mailing list). Tools support mixed strategies: authors invite reviewers, subscribe groups to receive notices, and tools (CodeCollaborator, Gerrit) can suggest or enforce reviewers based on recent file editors or component ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal number of reviewers (empirical finding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two reviewers find an optimal number of defects (empirical consensus and evidence from multiple projects/studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical inspection studies and the paper's empirical data indicate that two reviewers are often sufficient to find as many defects as larger teams; teams often invite 3–4 but the active median participation is two. Reducing reviewers without reducing defect-finding is a potential cost saving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review purpose / focus: group problem solving vs defect reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the activity focused on explicit defect recording or on discussing and fixing problems as a group?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary, asynchronous reviews shift from strict defect-finding to collaborative problem solving: reviewers comment on style, conventions, documentation, corner cases and suggest fixes; defects are often fixed rather than explicitly recorded. This change affects how effectiveness is measured and what tooling should support (discussion/resolution features rather than defect-count fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect measurement proxies: comments, comment threads, resubmissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because defects are not explicitly recorded in many contemporary tools, proxies are used: number of comments (upper bound), number of comment threads (better estimate), and number of artifact resubmissions (lower bound) per review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each proxy has assumptions and limitations: comments may cover the same defect (overestimate); threads are closer to distinct defects but can combine related issues or false positives; resubmissions indicate non-trivial fixes and are a conservative lower bound. The paper suggests combining these three proxies to approximate review effectiveness. Table 2 and Figures 6–7 provide medians per project (e.g., median comments per review: Chrome 4, Android 3, Bing 4, Office 3, SQL 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments per review (discussion volume)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of comments recorded during a review (used as an upper-bound proxy for defects/discussion intensity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Median comments per review reported: Chrome 4, Android 3, Bing 4, Office 3, SQL 3. Many comments are conversational and may not each represent distinct defects; still, comment volume indicates review activity and thoroughness of discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment threads and resolved threads
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of distinct comment threads and how many threads are marked resolved (used as proxy for distinct issues found and closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools that track thread resolution (CodeFlow) allow counting threads and threads marked resolved. Table 2 in the paper provides project quartiles for comments, threads, and resolved threads; resolved threads are used as a proxy for problems actually found and addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmissions per review
rubrics_metrics.description: How many times an artifact/change is resubmitted for review (used as a lower-bound proxy for number of substantive fixes required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A revised artifact may be resubmitted after fixes; resubmission counts underestimate total defects (one resubmission can fix multiple defects) but indicate presence of substantive corrections. Figure 7 shows distributions across projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge sharing metric (files known: submitted ∪ reviewed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does review spread knowledge about the system? Measured by number of distinct files a developer has modified (submitted) and/or reviewed, and the union (total files known).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend Mockus & Herbsleb's expertise measure: count files modified and files reviewed and report increases in 'files known' due to reviewing. Example medians: Chrome developer submits to 24 files, reviews 38 files, total 43 files — a 44% increase (19 fewer files without review). For Bing, Office, SQL, review increases files known by 100%, 122%, and 150% respectively. The metric can be refined (exclude tiny contributors, cap at 10 files per submission in the paper) and used to assess diversity and spread of knowledge in the team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool support and traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review tooling provide traceability, structured states, and features to support review workflows and implicit measures?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tool features matter: Gerrit centralizes Git with Verify/Approved/Submitted stages, CodeFlow stores comments, sign-offs, and thread statuses (open/ignored/resolved/closed), CodeCollaborator enforces rules (e.g., require 2 reviewers) and suggests reviewers. Tool-supported review is contrasted with mailing-list-based OSS review: tools make review traceable and automatically record metrics useful for empirical analysis and process improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative development / early review practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews are performed early (before the change is committed), quickly, and frequently as part of iterative development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary review steps summarized: (1) author creates and submits change, (2) developers discuss and suggest fixes (changes may be resubmitted multiple times), (3) one or more reviewers approve and the change is merged or rejected. This lightweight, flexible process contrasts with formal inspection meetings that review large completed artifacts and emphasizes small, frequent changes to support rapid integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid requiring explicit defect counts (process design consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mandating explicit defect-recording fields during review because this can distract reviewers from fixing defects and from the collaborative goal of making code acceptable before check-in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that in many projects explicit defect fields are unused (e.g., AMD: 87% of reviews have no recorded defects) and some tools (CodeFlow) do not provide defect-count fields by design. The anti-pattern is requiring defect logging that interrupts repair-oriented, conversational review; instead use non-intrusive proxies (comments, threads, resubmissions) or tool-supported thread resolution states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise / who-knows-what matters
rubrics_metrics.description: People- and product-level measures (reviewer expertise/history with files) are stronger predictors of defect-finding effectiveness than minor variations in the inspection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work (Porter et al.) and the paper highlight that expertise of reviewers and assignment of reviewers who have worked on the file recently (expertise browser / tool suggestions) are important factors affecting review effectiveness. Tools that surface past editors or component owners help select appropriate reviewers.
